Title: U.S. Energy Policy Pivots Towards Domestic Security | OilPrice.com

Summary: 
The new U.S. law, dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), sharply shifts energy policy toward domestic security by imposing aggressive foreign‑content tests and restrictions on foreign entities. The act shortens the eligibility period for Clean Electricity Production and Investment Tax Credits (45Y and 48E) to 12 months of construction and service by end‑2027, a drastic change from the IRA’s 2032 deadline. It also extends biofuel credits for several years while eliminating consumer‑facing credits for electric vehicles and residential solar. The OBBBA introduces a North American feedstock requirement for biofuels and sets domestic‑content thresholds that rise to as high as 90% for certain equipment, making compliance costly for solar developers. U.S. shale companies stand to benefit from a royalty‑rate cut and a reinstated 100% bonus depreciation, which Rystad estimates could lower breakeven prices by one to two dollars per barrel for short‑term development in core unconventional plays. The law’s overall effect is to accelerate the transition away from wind, solar, and clean hydrogen subsidies while bolstering traditional fuels and domestic supply chains.

Title: New risks for U.S. solar

Summary: 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), enacted in July 2025, introduces significant changes to U.S. solar and energy storage tax incentives, extending full 100% investment tax credit (ITC) and production tax credit (PTC) eligibility through 2030 for projects beginning construction by mid-2026. Projects must be placed in service by the end of 2027 to access 48E/45Y credits, with a four-year completion window for those starting within 12 months of the law’s enactment. The OBBBA removes the proposed foreign entity of concern (FEOC) excise tax but retains FEOC restrictions, including ownership, material assistance, and foreign influence rules. Material assistance provisions apply from January 1, 2026, with projects starting in 2025 eligible for full credits through 2029, while those starting in the first half of 2026 qualify through 2030 with restrictions. Projects starting in the second half of 2026 must be in service by 2027 to claim full value. Storage is now included in the domestic content step-up for 48E. Projects on Bureau of Land Management (BLM) lands must allocate at least 20% of costs to on-site activities to qualify for full 48E credit, increasing compliance complexity. Title: Steel Production Expansion through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Summary: 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law on July 4, 2025, expands Section 45X of the Internal Revenue Code to grant a 2.5 % production tax credit for metallurgical coal (met‑coal) used in steelmaking from 2026 through 2029, ending on December 31, 2029. The credit is a short‑term incentive designed to spur immediate investment in production capacity rather than a long‑term subsidy. The Act does not impose a domestic‑production requirement; producers may mine coal inside or outside the United States provided it is sold to an ‘unrelated person’. A sales‑structure provision ensures that if a related entity sells to an unrelated buyer, the transaction is treated as a direct sale for credit eligibility. The credit still requires the claimant to be a U.S. taxpayer and the sale to be to an unrelated party, thereby preserving a U.S. nexus and benefiting U.S. companies by lowering after‑tax production costs.

The legislation follows the Department of Energy’s May 29, 2025 designation of metallurgical coal as a ‘critical material’ (90 Fed. Reg. 22711) to support U.S. steel dominance. The OBBBA’s definition of ‘metallurgical coal’ is simply ‘coal suitable for use in the production of steel,’ but the statute does not set purity or testing thresholds, leaving the criteria for suitability ambiguous. Opponents argue that met‑coal, as a fuel material, does not meet the legal definition of a critical material because it faces a lower risk of supply‑chain disruption.

Unlike other critical minerals that receive a phased‑out credit schedule through 2033, the met‑coal credit ends entirely in 2029, making it a potentially broad but time‑limited incentive. The Act’s lack of a domestic‑production requirement and the global eligibility of coal raise policy concerns about subsidizing foreign production while still aiming to strengthen domestic supply chains. Industry participants are urged to understand the credit mechanics, structure transactions accordingly, and prepare for further regulatory clarification before the 2029 expiration.

Title: Inflation Reduction Act Would Significantly Expand Federal Income Tax Benefits for Green Technology Industry

Summary: 
The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 expands federal income‑tax benefits for green‑technology projects.  It extends the existing Section 45 PTC and Section 48 ITC for wind and solar facilities, adds the PTC to new solar projects, and removes sunset provisions for facilities placed in service after 2021.  The Act introduces a new Section 45Y clean‑electricity production credit (CEPTC) and a Section 48D clean‑electricity investment credit (CEITC) that apply to any renewable or energy‑storage facility that begins construction after 2025, with rates tied to a 0 % greenhouse‑gas‑emissions standard.  Energy‑storage facilities gain an election out of the public‑utility property limitation and are treated as five‑year property under MACRS.  The Act also expands the ITC/PTC to energy‑storage, biogas, microgrid controller equipment, and provides a separate PTC for electricity used to produce clean hydrogen under Section 45V.  Wage‑and‑apprenticeship standards can trigger an 80 % credit haircut, while meeting domestic‑content or energy‑community standards can add a 10 % (or 20 % for low‑income communities) credit enhancement.  The Section 45Q carbon‑capture credit is extended to facilities beginning construction before 2033, with a higher rate for direct‑air‑capture.  Fuel‑production credits are extended through 2024 and a new Section 45Z clean‑fuel credit is introduced for 2025‑2027.  The dormant Section 48C investment credit is revived for advanced‑energy production and manufacturing, with a $10 billion ceiling.  The Act creates refundable credits for tax‑exempt entities, allows sale of refundable credits, and changes carry‑over rules to a 3‑year carryback and 22‑year carryforward.  These provisions aim to streamline compliance, incentivize domestic content, and broaden financing options for green projects.

Title: Analysis of Renewable Energy Credit Amendments and Changes Under the 2025 Tax Legislation

Summary: 
The 2025 Tax Legislation has made significant changes to the Renewable Energy Credit provisions, including the adoption of 'prohibited foreign entity' rules and 'material assistance' rules. The prohibited foreign entity rules prevent certain entities owned or controlled by foreign governments or companies from claiming renewable energy credits. The material assistance rules prevent eligibility for certain credits where a prohibited foreign entity has materially assisted with manufacturing or construction. The Legislation also terminates the clean electricity production credit and investment tax credit for wind and solar energy property placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027, but with a one-year delay for projects that begin construction within the next year. The Legislation contains revisions to Section 45X, including amendments to the definition of 'battery module' and the addition of phaseouts to Section 45X tax credits for the production of critical minerals starting in 2031. The prohibited foreign entity rules also prohibit any manufacturer that meets the definition of 'prohibited foreign entity' from claiming a Section 45X credit. The material assistance rules also apply to prohibit any property manufactured with the material assistance of a prohibited foreign entity from qualifying as an eligible component for purposes of Section 45X. The Legislation repeals several other IRA credits, including the Section 25E credits for previously owned clean vehicles and the Section 30D clean vehicle credit. The Legislation also increases the advanced manufacturing tax credit, including for semiconductor manufacturers, from 25 percent to 35 percent for certain new facilities.

Title: IRS Issues Final Regulations For Mandatory Roth Catch-Up Contributions

Summary: 
The Treasury Department and the IRS have issued final regulations on the SECURE 2.0 Act’s mandatory Roth catch‑up provisions. Under the new rules, employees aged 50 or older who earned at least $145,000 in FICA wages the previous year must treat any catch‑up contribution to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457(b) plan as an after‑tax Roth contribution. The regulations also clarify that the Roth catch‑up requirement applies to taxable years beginning after December 31 2026, meaning it takes effect in 2027. Plans may adopt the requirement for earlier years if they use a reasonable, good‑faith interpretation of the statute, but they are not required to change until 2027. The final rules provide guidance on higher catch‑up limits for employees aged 60‑63 and for newly established SIMPLE plans. The SECURE 2.0 Act itself expanded catch‑up limits, broadened eligibility for part‑time workers, allowed employers to match student‑loan payments, added emergency withdrawal provisions for domestic‑violence victims, and altered required minimum distributions. The proposed rules were released on January 10 2025, and the final regulations incorporate changes made in response to comments. The administrative transition period for 2024‑2025 remains unchanged, ending December 31 2025. "The big change is timing," the article notes, "the final regulations make clear that provisions relating to the Roth catch‑up requirement generally apply to contributions in taxable years beginning after December 31 2026."

The IRS is phasing out paper tax refund checks starting September 30, 2025, under President Trump’s Executive Order, though lawmakers from Maine and New Hampshire urged a delay, citing risks to vulnerable populations and rural communities. The IRS has extended a deferred resignation offer to employees on administrative leave for the third time, with no disclosure on the number of acceptances. U.S. multinational companies are urging faster OECD Pillar Two negotiations, warning that delays could impose high compliance costs without a 'side-by-side' exception for the U.S. system. Some countries, including France, Spain, and Kenya, have maintained digital services taxes (DSTs), while India and Canada repealed theirs under U.S. pressure. The Treasury and IRS expect to release four pieces of international tax guidance by year-end, covering FDDEI, controlled foreign corporations, and foreign-earned income credits. The permanent extension of 100% bonus depreciation under OBBBA, costing $362.7 billion over 10 years, has drawn criticism from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), who asked the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) to detail its beneficiaries and impacts. The Senate Finance Committee held a hearing on digital asset taxation on October 1, 2025.

articles.title: Inflation Reduction Act Would Significantly Expand Federal Income Tax Benefits for Green Technology Industry
articles.summary: The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 expands federal income‑tax benefits for green‑technology projects.  It extends the existing Section 45 PTC and Section 48 ITC for wind and solar facilities, adds the PTC to new solar projects, and removes sunset provisions for facilities placed in service after 2021.  The Act introduces a new Section 45Y clean‑electricity production credit (CEPTC) and a Section 48D clean‑electricity investment credit (CEITC) that apply to any renewable or energy‑storage facility that begins construction after 2025, with rates tied to a 0 % greenhouse‑gas‑emissions standard.  Energy‑storage facilities gain an election out of the public‑utility property limitation and are treated as five‑year property under MACRS.  The Act also expands the ITC/PTC to energy‑storage, biogas, microgrid controller equipment, and provides a separate PTC for electricity used to produce clean hydrogen under Section 45V.  Wage‑and‑apprenticeship standards can trigger an 80 % credit haircut, while meeting domestic‑content or energy‑community standards can add a 10 % (or 20 % for low‑income communities) credit enhancement.  The Section 45Q carbon‑capture credit is extended to facilities beginning construction before 2033, with a higher rate for direct‑air‑capture.  Fuel‑production credits are extended through 2024 and a new Section 45Z clean‑fuel credit is introduced for 2025‑2027.  The dormant Section 48C investment credit is revived for advanced‑energy production and manufacturing, with a $10 billion ceiling.  The Act creates refundable credits for tax‑exempt entities, allows sale of refundable credits, and changes carry‑over rules to a 3‑year carryback and 22‑year carryforward.  These provisions aim to streamline compliance, incentivize domestic content, and broaden financing options for green projects.

articles.title: Clean Energy Tax Credit Changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act
articles.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) has made significant changes to the clean energy tax credits previously enacted under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. The OBBBA limits future opportunities for wind and solar projects, requiring them to be placed in service by December 31, 2027, to remain eligible for tax credits. A safe harbor is available for projects that begin construction on or before July 4, 2026. The OBBBA also introduces domestic content requirements, raising the minimum from 40% to 45% for projects beginning construction after June 12, 2025, and incrementally thereafter up to 55% starting in 2027. The credit for sequestration of carbon oxides has been increased to $85 per metric ton, and Code Sections 45Z and 40A have been extended to permit small agri-biodiesel producers to receive credits for sales taking place on or prior to December 31, 2026. The OBBBA also takes a strong stance against the ownership, control, and influence of clean energy projects by North Korea, China, Russia, and Iran, prohibiting tax credits for 'specified foreign entities' and 'foreign-influenced entities.'

articles.title: Analysis of Renewable Energy Credit Amendments and Changes Under the 2025 Tax Legislation
articles.summary: The 2025 Tax Legislation has made significant changes to the Renewable Energy Credit provisions, including the adoption of 'prohibited foreign entity' rules and 'material assistance' rules. The prohibited foreign entity rules prevent certain entities owned or controlled by foreign governments or companies from claiming renewable energy credits. The material assistance rules prevent eligibility for certain credits where a prohibited foreign entity has materially assisted with manufacturing or construction. The Legislation also terminates the clean electricity production credit and investment tax credit for wind and solar energy property placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027, but with a one-year delay for projects that begin construction within the next year. The Legislation contains revisions to Section 45X, including amendments to the definition of 'battery module' and the addition of phaseouts to Section 45X tax credits for the production of critical minerals starting in 2031. The prohibited foreign entity rules also prohibit any manufacturer that meets the definition of 'prohibited foreign entity' from claiming a Section 45X credit. The material assistance rules also apply to prohibit any property manufactured with the material assistance of a prohibited foreign entity from qualifying as an eligible component for purposes of Section 45X. The Legislation repeals several other IRA credits, including the Section 25E credits for previously owned clean vehicles and the Section 30D clean vehicle credit. The Legislation also increases the advanced manufacturing tax credit, including for semiconductor manufacturers, from 25 percent to 35 percent for certain new facilities.

articles.title: IRS Issues Final Regulations For Mandatory Roth Catch-Up Contributions
articles.summary: The Treasury Department and the IRS have issued final regulations on the SECURE 2.0 Act’s mandatory Roth catch‑up provisions. Under the new rules, employees aged 50 or older who earned at least $145,000 in FICA wages the previous year must treat any catch‑up contribution to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457(b) plan as an after‑tax Roth contribution. The regulations also clarify that the Roth catch‑up requirement applies to taxable years beginning after December 31 2026, meaning it takes effect in 2027. Plans may adopt the requirement for earlier years if they use a reasonable, good‑faith interpretation of the statute, but they are not required to change until 2027. The final rules provide guidance on higher catch‑up limits for employees aged 60‑63 and for newly established SIMPLE plans. The SECURE 2.0 Act itself expanded catch‑up limits, broadened eligibility for part‑time workers, allowed employers to match student‑loan payments, added emergency withdrawal provisions for domestic‑violence victims, and altered required minimum distributions. The proposed rules were released on January 10 2025, and the final regulations incorporate changes made in response to comments. The administrative transition period for 2024‑2025 remains unchanged, ending December 31 2025. "The big change is timing," the article notes, "the final regulations make clear that provisions relating to the Roth catch‑up requirement generally apply to contributions in taxable years beginning after December 31 2026."
